items.en: On the night of October 11 to 12, 2026, fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets started to warm up. Cyber attackers had pushed the refrigeration systems into defrost mode, which heats the cooling parts to melt ice. Some units reached 50°C (122°F), some equipment started to catch fire, according to the Paris prosecutor, and stores threw away their fresh and frozen food. The reports pointed to one maker of refrigeration controllers, Danfoss (a Danish industrial company).
We went through IPinfo's weekly Internet scans to examine these systems before the attack. In this blog post we’ll explore some of the findings. Here’s the TL;DR:

The numbers from the chains keep growing. More than 400 stores were hit in total according to Futura-Sciences, and losses could reach several million euros. Carrefour said 80 of its stores were hit, while Intermarché and Netto, both part of Les Mousquetaires (a French retail group), had more than 300 hit. Monoprix reported that about 5% of its stores were affected.

Leclerc and Coopérative U, two other French supermarket chains, also confirmed attacks. Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that 80 of its 2,000 stores were hit. He added that the stores don't buy from Danfoss directly but use a Danfoss system supplied by their refrigeration contractors.

Danfoss said most of the affected equipment was "legacy,” naming two older controller models, the AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355. CERT-FR (France's cybersecurity agency) said it knew of numerous compromises of AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. It told operators to disconnect them or restrict who can reach them, and updated its alert on October 13 to add XWEB supervisors (systems that monitor a store's fridges and freezers) from Copeland, a US maker of cooling equipment, and Dixell, its Italian brand. Its alert says attack campaigns are probably still ongoing. Nobody has said who did it or how they got in, and the Paris prosecutor's office has opened an investigation.

We scan the IPv4 Internet (the most common type of Internet address) every week, connecting to the usual ports that websites use (the numbered doors a computer answers on) and recording what answers. In the sweep that ran on October 6 and 7, five days before the attack, 2,528 addresses showed a Danfoss StoreView dashboard. That is the web page that stores and technicians use to watch and manage these controllers, the equivalent of the control panel in the back room, except that anyone who typed in the address could open it.

According to our data, France had 1,331 of them (53%). That is more than the other 72 countries and territories combined (1,197). Poland came next with 179, then the United States (101), Portugal (92), and Belgium (85).

Why France? Our data can't say, but it rules a few things out. French dashboards ran the same mix of software versions as everywhere else, so they weren't patched worse. They also weren't unusual in how they connect. In France, about two-thirds connect through one national provider, much like the main telecom in Portugal, Germany, or Romania. Almost all (98%) are on telecom providers' networks rather than in data centers or clouds, which fits a controller plugged into the store's own Internet connection, with access opened for a technician or head office.
CERT-FR's advice hints at why stores keep them online: it tells them to check their insurance terms before cutting the data their controllers send to refrigeration contractors.

The dashboards also give away how old the software behind them is. They come in two generations. The older one is a page built with Flash (an old browser plug-in, retired in 2020) and served by the AK-SM 800. Danfoss declared these controllers end of life in 2023. That same year, the security firm Synacktiv published a login bypass (a way in without the password) for them, and Danfoss's advice was to restrict network access. This is the "legacy" equipment Danfoss named.

The newer one runs on the AK-SM 800A, Danfoss's current model. Its dashboard shows when its software was built, a bit like the production date stamped on a carton, which tells us roughly which version it runs: 242 of them say May 19, 2023, the build date of firmware 3.3 (firmware is the software built into the controller). Controllers older than 3.3 miss three 2023 fixes, including one for a flaw rated critical. Those older than 4.2 also miss a fix for a 2025 login bypass, and those older than 4.3.1 miss two more 2025 fixes.

Put together, 85% of the French dashboards (1,136 of 1,331) ran software with known security flaws, almost the same as the 84% elsewhere. That is 527 older controllers Danfoss no longer supports, 280 missing the 2023 fixes, and 329 missing the 2025 fixes. Only 195 had every known fix.
Every scan from late March 2026 until the attack found about the same number: between 2,464 and 2,622 Danfoss dashboards open to the Internet, roughly half of them in France.

They were mostly the same devices. Of the 1,331 French dashboards found on October 6, 1,019 were open at the very same address on March 30, six months earlier. Over those months, the number of older controllers Danfoss no longer supports didn't go down in France (519 at the end of March, 527 in October). Updates came slowly. The share of newer French controllers with every known fix went from 14% to 24%, under two points a month.

Most stores did disconnect after the attack. Our next weekly scan ran on October 14, two days after the attack. Of the 1,331 French dashboards from October 6–7, only 316 were still online at the same address, a 76% drop. In the weekly scans from August to early October, only 3% to 7% disappeared from one week to the next. The older controllers Danfoss no longer supports fell the most, from 527 to 64. Fully updated ones fell too, from 195 to 54, which points to stores disconnecting them rather than updating them.

Outside France, 25% disappeared, more than the usual 9% to 12%. Censys, another Internet scanning company that counts every day, saw a similar 71% drop in France between October 11 and 14. On October 14, the technical director of Claroty, the security company that found the 2025 flaws, told Tom's Guide that exposed AK-SM 800 controllers were still online. Our October 14 scan still found 64 of them.

France wasn't the only country with these systems online. Danfoss dashboards with known flaws were open in 69 other countries and territories, led by Poland (157), the United States (85), and Portugal (77). In some countries most were the older controllers Danfoss no longer supports: 80% in Iceland, 75% in Australia, and 72% in Germany.

Some reports suggest other European countries may have been hit. One analyst quoted by Australia's ABC said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium had also been affected. Our data can't say whether they were, but it does show that all five had out-of-date Danfoss dashboards open to the Internet five days before the attack.

CERT-FR's updated alert also names XWEB supervisors from Dixell, Copeland's Italian brand of refrigeration controllers, so we counted those too. The same scan found 1,611 XWEB dashboards in 66 countries, but only 70 in France; Italy, where Dixell is based, had 467. Judging by when their software was built, only 180 of the 752 newer XWEB PRO units had the February 2026 fixes. The other 859 were older models that haven't had a software update from Copeland since 2018. After the attack, French operators unplugged their XWEB dashboards too: our October 14 scan found only 20 of the 70 still online, a 71% drop, when a normal week loses 2% to 9%. Elsewhere, including Italy, the number fell only at the usual weekly rate.

The dashboards were identified with two fingerprints (patterns that identify a device) built by our data team. The newer interface is matched by its page title. The older one is matched by its web server plus the Flash loader page, which identifies the AK-SM 800. AK-SC 355 controllers, which Danfoss also named, may not be in our count. Sixteen devices that share the older web server but aren't Danfoss (network cards in backup power units, building controllers, thermostats) were removed, along with two addresses that answer on almost every port, a sign of a honeypot (a decoy set up to attract attackers).

An independent count by the security researcher Baptiste Robert, posted on X, found 2,752 Danfoss systems online, 1,590 of them in France, a little above ours. Censys, which scans differently, found more: 1,825 of the newer dashboards in France on October 11, 61% of its worldwide total.

The numbers are a minimum. They cover IPv4 only and the ports we scan, and an address is not always one store. We aren't publishing any of the addresses. CERT-FR told us it had already identified the affected systems, and we're in contact with CERT-EU (the EU's cybersecurity team for its institutions) to help other European cybersecurity teams in any way we can.

CERT-FR's advice is to take these controllers off the public Internet and, if a contractor needs remote access, to give it through a secure VPN (a private, encrypted connection). Letting in only the contractor's addresses is a stopgap, not a fix. A factory reset alone isn't enough either: an exposed controller that no longer gets updates will likely be compromised again. For Danfoss systems, CERT-FR also says to update the firmware, set the security level to Strict, and change the default passwords.

We can't tell from the scans how the attackers got in or who they were, and we don't know which chains or stores were hit. Being able to open a dashboard from the Internet doesn't mean anyone can break in through it, and nobody has said whether any of the flaws above were used.

The data does show what things looked like before and after the attack. Five days before the attack, France had more of these dashboards open to anyone than the rest of the world combined, and most were behind on updates. After the attack, most of them went offline within days, and we'll keep checking the 316 that were still online on October 14.

This is one of IPinfo's data stories, where we use our own measurements to look at what happens on the Internet. If you spot something we got wrong, have data that adds to this, or have a story you'd like us to look into, write to us at emot@ipinfo.io.
Data: IPinfo's Internet scans of IPv4 addresses, October 6–7, 2026, and 18 weekly scans from March 30 to October 6, 2026. Counts are addresses and a minimum.

João Tomé is an Internet Data Research Editor at IPinfo, finding trends and stories about how the Internet works and changes. He has a background in journalism, data storytelling, and podcasting, including five years at Cloudflare.
A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale announced a $45 billion compute deal. Now, the duo may be about to do it again.

Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still under way and that the details could change.

If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year. TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.

The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors, who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.

Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported today that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.

Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.

But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.

The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.

Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.

Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.

These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn.

If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans.

The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.

That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.
Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.

These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.
Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype
Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

There is one person in the White House who deserves the most blame for the five-day tenure of Katie Zacharia, the not-ready-for-prime-time White House press secretary. That’s Donald Trump, who hired Zacharia with barely any vetting and gave her little time to prepare for her first briefing, which turned out to be a disaster.

But Team Trump isn’t big on faulting the president for anything. And sure enough, a Trump ally is now pointing the finger at “Zacharia’s allies,” telling Politico Playbook that she was used as a “pawn” in Trumpworld infighting:

One person close to the president blamed Zacharia’s allies for the turmoil that’s unfolded around her short tenure as press secretary. “The people around her are doing her a disservice and using her as a pawn in their own self-interest,” the person said. “It’s disgusting.”

The source did not elaborate on whom exactly they were referring to, but disagreement between White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Trump’s top aide, Natalie Harp, has been a recurring theme in all the gossip about her disastrous tenure.

Shortly before Zacharia’s first press conference, The Daily Mail reported that Trump had “blindsided his own West Wing” by hiring the conservative cable pundit as Karoline Leavitt’s replacement without even consulting Wiles. Axios later reported, “Zacharia’s hiring was solely a Trump decision, one furthered along with the strong input of his personal assistant Natalie Harp.”
Wiles raised no objections because “she knew the press secretary job is a personal one for the president,” per Axios. However, The Daily Mail reported that she saw Zacharia’s appointment as a defeat:

White House insiders told the Daily Mail Wiles accepted she lost this personnel battle and one administration source called it the latest in a string of ‘micro aggressions’ from the president toward his chief of staff.

The scope of these “micro aggressions” became clearer on Thursday. The lead story in Playbook was about Trump polling his allies on whether he should fire Wiles over issues unrelated to Zacharia. That prospect seemed to excite some in the White House:
Trump has been soliciting allies’ views of Wiles and musing about replacements for his top aide, according to four people with direct knowledge of the conversations.

We’re told Trump is getting plenty of encouragement from rivals to Wiles and people who’ve felt “burned” by his loyal enforcer. Some have been sharing unfavorable coverage of Wiles and her family (more on that below) with the president.
“She’s burned a lot of people,” a Republican operative close to the White House said.
A day later, Playbook reported that the story had caused a “freakout” in the White House. It said Harp had brought the negative Wiles coverage to Trump’s attention:

PLAYBOOK IN PRINT: Natalie Harp printed a copy of yesterday’s Playbook about Susie Wiles’ future for President Donald Trump, according to two people with knowledge. It caused a “freakout,” as three people described it to Playbook. The president “blew up” over more bad headlines about his chief of staff, and Wiles and allies “burn[ed] up phones around town” trying to quell the situation.
…. The president made more calls to allies about Wiles after reading Playbook, according to a person with direct knowledge.

The Trump administration strongly denied both Playbook reports. In a statement, the president called the story “TOTAL FAKE NEWS,” and heaped praise on his chief of staff, saying, “Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that. She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”

When they weren’t (allegedly) freaking out about the Wiles drama last week, White House staffers were watching Zacharia dig herself a deeper hole as she tried to explain why she said she passed the bar in China when it turned out she hadn’t passed it at all.

One White House staffer was in Zacharia’s corner, even after her terrible introduction. According to the New York Times, “While Ms. Zacharia did have the support of Natalie Harp, the powerful West Wing aide who rarely leaves the president’s side, others in the building believed her debut had been a disaster.”

But any doubts about Zacharia’s impending doom were removed when she stumbled through a highly unusual grilling from Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Thursday night. Zacharia was fired on Friday while she was in the middle of an interview with The Wall Street Journal. Hours later, Politico reported that the Hannity debacle was a “sanctioned hit” courtesy of Wiles:
One of the people, granted anonymity to discuss internal dynamics, described the appearance as a “sanctioned hit” on Zacharia, who was not Wiles’ preferred choice for the role.
“[White House spokesperson] Danielle [Alvarez] and Susie fed her to Hannity,” a second person familiar with the matter said, noting that Wiles and Hannity are friendly and speak often.

A senior White House official disputed this, saying, “Susie and Sean do talk, but Susie did not need to feed her to Sean or anybody else. It’s not her style.” They also asserted that the real “nail in her coffin” wasn’t Hannity but another awful appearance on Friday’s Fox & Friends.

Further reporting from the New York Post undermined claims that the Hannity appearance was orchestrated by Wiles. Texts obtained by the outlet show Zacharia was setting up the interviews with Fox’s bookers as early as Tuesday, apparently without the chief of staff’s involvement.
That doesn’t prove Wiles had no hand in the tone of the Fox hosts’ questioning. But the White House told the Post that claims Wiles was involved in taking down Zacharia were “hit jobs” and “smear.”

Even if Zacharia ouster wasn’t the result of some proxy battle between Harp and Wiles, this isn’t the first hint that there may be tension between two of the Trump administration’s most powerful figures.
A source told Regime Change authors Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan that Wiles was stunned when she learned Harp had written Trump adoring letters, asking herself, “Where am I?”

In May, Harp was publicly blamed for two of Trump’s most incendiary Truth Social posts — the racist Obama meme and the Trump-as-Jesus image — in a Wall Street Journal report that cited “people familiar with the matter.” The piece said Harp had made herself some enemies in the White House by circumventing the chief of staff’s office, among others:

Harp has frustrated some White House officials because she typically doesn’t share draft posts with the chief of staff’s office, communications aides or national-security officials. Harp has told others she works for Trump and only listens to him.

Last month, multiple reports said Harp instigated Trump’s White House press ban by bringing negative media coverage to his attention. The Journal’s coverage noted that the debacle got started while Wiles was away from the White House, suggesting it was the result of Trump and Harp being left to their own devices.

Wiles, who doesn’t give many on-the-record interviews, hasn’t said anything publicly about Trump’s “human printer.” As for Harp, she praised Wiles last month in a weird email interview with Washingtonian:
4. Who are one or two women whom you admire or who have been a role model or mentor to you?

Success is determined not just by what is achieved, but under what circumstances. Fighting cancer while serving as Chief of Staff for the Most Consequential President in History, Susie Wiles is an example to all of what can be accomplished when one has the strength and resolve to do so. …

The White House referred the Daily Beast to this interview when asked over the weekend if there’s a rift between Harp and Wiles. People never turn on their mentor, using their own tricks against them, so it sounds like everything is actually fine!
- Zacharia Out as Press Secretary in Half a Scaramucci
Aging is the price paid for the ability of experiencing existence, one might philosophize.

Natural cellular aging begins with differentiation. Once a stem cell becomes a specific cell type, it's locked in forever: fat cells can never become muscle cells, no matter how hard one wishes, or pokes and prods at them in front of the mirror.
Or so it goes in nature, but scientists can definitely transform cells, as if biologically compensating for all the failed alchemical attempts of the past.
Now, scientists have transformed old blood cells into young brain stem cells, which continued to grow younger as they grew older.
The researchers, from the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn, in Germany, described their methods in the journal Aging Cell.

Cellular transformations can be done in two main ways. The first, more circuitous route turns a specific cell back into a pluripotent stem cell, or an embryonic "blank slate," and then into a different cell type.
The second method involves a "direct conversion," which skips the middle stage and directly transforms a cell into a different type.

"Using this method, we have directly converted red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells," summarizes Oliver Brüstle, the director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn.
The researchers used donor cells from 15 people across the age spectrum, from newborn to 101 years of age.

They specifically took erythroid progenitor cells (EPCs), which are akin to red blood cells that haven't graduated college yet, and turned them into induced neural stem cells (iNSCs), which are the pre-graduate cells of the brain.
They achieved the direct conversion genetic shortcut via an unlikely agent that usually destroys cells.
The researchers used a virus to deliver two transcription factors, or proteins that attach to DNA to regulate gene activity, to get the cells to change their types.
Then they used two genome-bloodhounding methods – DNA methylation measures and RNA sequencing – to track the resultant anti-aging effects and genetic behavior.
By the 12th day after the viral "infection," the cells started showing their new identity, ditching their blood-like proteins and replacing them with the expression of neural-like proteins instead.
Initially, the epigenetic age (the DNA changes accumulated over time) of the EPCs was highly correlated with the chronological age of their donors.
Obviously, blank slate cells revert to an embryonic state and become rejuvenated, regardless of the age of the person who donated the blood sample.
So the researchers wanted to see if the direct conversion method they used also rejuvenated the converted cells.
Intriguingly, they did, though it took more than twice as long.
But this was just the appetizer, because the neuronal stem cells kept getting younger as they got older (excuse the paradox).

Over the following 50 to 100 days, they kept de-aging, eventually reaching about 5 percent of the donor age, with the majority of epigenetic age-related traits resetting by around 50 days of the conversion process.
In other words, counter-intuitively, they got younger as they got older.

In effect, the converted cells became 60 years younger in 50 days, the researchers note in their official statement, proving that you really can 'melt away the years' as hotel-spa brochures and late-night infomercials promise (if you're a cell, anyway).
But were these cells actually younger, or did they just look that way? In other words, anyone can slip on a Thrasher hoodie, but it doesn't imbue them with skate-worthy balance.
"We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells," Brüstle says.
The researchers analyzed this through numerous measures, including protein expression as well as the rejuvenated cells' recycling abilities.
The cells also displayed less DNA damage and mitochondrial toxicity, showing that the direct conversion cells enjoyed benefits comparable to the blank slate cells.

Intriguingly, they continued growing biologically younger even in conditions that inhibited their proliferation, or ability to divide and multiply, suggesting their rejuvenation isn't dependent on their ability to split.

The researchers do mention some study limitations. These include potential mathematical biases in de-aging models, the absence of naturally aged neural stem cells to use as comparisons, and potential in vitro versus in vivo behavioral differences in cells.

But, promisingly, engineered cells appear to be viable. In previous Franken-mouse-like research from Bonn scientists, cells formed connections with existing neural cells after being transplanted into the brains of mice.
Such GMO mice à la Pinky and the Brain demonstrate future therapeutic value, suggesting the possibility of engineering brain cells for individuals affected by neurodegeneration.
Finally, the protracted nature of the converted cells in this work allows easier study:
"Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model," Brüstle emphasizes.
"Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process."
The research has been published in Aging Cell.

The Air Force is investigating after a Tactical Air Control Party instructor died Oct. 17 from injuries suffered during what appeared to be an uncontrolled descent during a rappelling demonstration at a college football game in San Antonio, Texas.

Officials identified the deceased Airman as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a member of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, according to an Oct. 18 Air Force press release. The unit focuses on training Airmen to become TACPs and other joint fires integrators such as joint terminal attack controllers, air liaison officers, ground liaison officers, and air support operations center personnel to embed with Army and Marine units to coordinate and deconflict all surface and air fires on the battlefield.

The accident occurred as Patterson was participating in a pregame rappelling demonstration from the ceiling of the Alamodome stadium before the University of Texas-San Antonio played Navy as part of its Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night, KSAT reported. After his fall, Patterson received medical attention on the field and was transported to a local hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.
The details surrounding the cause of Patterson’s death remain under investigation, according to a spokesperson for the 57th Wing, which oversees the 6th Combat Training Squadron.

“To maintain the integrity and impartiality of the ongoing investigation, [we] cannot address specific questions, operational details, or speculative scenarios at this time, as doing so could impede the investigative process,” the spokesperson said.

Video of the accident circulated on social media appears to show Patterson descending rapidly down the rappel rope without braking before he impacted with the ground. Military rappelers slow their descent by braking—a technique where the service member presses their dominant hand holding the free end of the rope against the hip or the small of the back.

This is not the first time miliary personnel have rappelled from the Alamodome’s ceiling. In 2013, instructors from the Army’s 101st Airborne Division Air Assault School from Fort Campbell, Ky., conducted a pregame rappelling demonstration inside the stadium before the U.S. Army All-American Bowl game.

The Alamodome’s 180-foot ceiling is more than double the height of most military rappel towers, which range from 34 feet to 90 feet. But some personnel have rappelled from helicopters hovering above 200 feet.

Rappelling from such heights can create increased friction that can cause the rappelers’ hands to heat up. While practicing for the 2013 event, 101st instructors “complained about their hands feeling pretty warm, despite wearing gloves,” according to an Army release from the time. After their first practice rappel, the Soldiers added special inserts into their gloves to protect their hands from the heat buildup.
It’s unclear if Patterson, who was one of four service members participating in the Oct. 17 demonstration, practiced rappelling from the stadium’s ceiling before the event, KSAT.com reported.

Patterson became a decorated Airman during his 15 years of service. In 2022, he was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to the Oct. 18 press release. Patterson’s other decorations included the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters, the Army Commendation Medal, Air and Space Achievement Medal, and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster, according to the release.
Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, who commands the 57th Wing, called Patterson’s death a “profound loss.”

“This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing,” Mills said in the release. “Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him.”

When the trio of NASA’s SkyFall helicopters takes to the Martian skies, one of their tasks will be to hunt for frozen water — a critical resource for future astronauts — using ground-penetrating radar. For that radar to work, each rotorcraft will carry a flexible, fabric-based antenna that will need to extend below the aircraft without interfering with landings or breaking upon impact. It is a specialized design for the mission, and it recently cleared a round of testing at the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

Although orbiting spacecraft can map the thick Martian ice deposits tens of yards below the surface, they’re effectively blind to the top several yards of regolith, or broken rock and dust. This shallow zone is what will matter most for future astronauts, who will need to easily reach and process ice for water, oxygen, and fuel.

“The only way to detect shallow subsurface ice remotely is to fly close to the ground,” said Adrian Tang, SkyFall’s ground-penetrating radar lead instrument scientist at JPL. “By flying low and slow, a SkyFall helicopter could capture radar images that resolve the fine layering where dry soil gives way to ice, detecting its presence and mapping its extent.”

To peer beneath the Martian surface, SkyFall’s ground-penetrating radar will use an ultra-wide frequency range — from 500 to 2,500 megahertz — corresponding to wavelengths of about 24 to 5 inches (60 to 12 centimeters). The longest wavelengths can penetrate several yards below the surface. The shorter wavelengths provide finer detail about the uppermost layers and surface texture.

This is where the unique antenna design comes in. A traditional antenna operating in that part of the electromagnetic spectrum would need to be 19 inches (48.3 centimeters) long and have a clear view of the ground, but the minimum clearance between Mars’ surface and the base of the helicopter’s fuselage is only about 6 inches (15.2 centimeters). The team needed an antenna that wouldn’t interfere with or be damaged by landing.

After an extensive search for the right antenna, the SkyFall team zeroed in on the Vivaldi because it can transmit and receive signals across a large, continuous range of radio frequencies, and because its flat, lightweight profile can be easily cut into flexible, metalized fabrics. The curvilinear antenna was named by its inventor, Peter Gibson, who felt its sweeping lines resembled a violin, an instrument associated with composer Antonio Vivaldi.

While the standard Vivaldi footprint was efficient and robust, it was still too large to work with SkyFall’s ground clearance. Fortunately, SkyFall’s ground-penetrating radar can be further miniaturized because it is designed specifically for shallow surveying (under 16 feet, or 5 meters) in the dry Martian regolith, which blocks radio waves far less than Earth’s soil. The team developed techniques to reduce the antenna’s size even more without sacrificing sensitivity.

“Although we managed to shrink the antenna quite a bit, it is about 1½ times longer than the helicopter’s legs,” said Christine Gebara, SkyFall ground-penetrating radar mechanical lead at JPL. “That means during landing, the Vivaldi has to bend out of the way — and if it lands on a rock, it bends even further. But when the helicopter takes off again, the antenna must spring back into place for data collection. Because SkyFall is expected to make dozens of flights exploring Mars, we needed an antenna that could repeatedly handle those pressures without losing its shape in flight.”

To ensure their downsized Vivaldi could withstand flight operations, the team sheathed it in a polyester and then layers of Vectran — the same flexible, superstrong material used for the landing airbags containing NASA’s Spirit and Opportunity Mars rovers. To help the antenna maintain shape while airborne, engineers added flexible fiberglass tape springs and a lightweight magnesium mounting structure. The entire setup weighs about 5 ounces (150 grams), slightly more than two violin bows.

Testing space hardware concepts with paper designs and mathematical models can get a mission only so far. The team needed to prove their antenna prototype could survive a full mission’s worth of intense temperature swings and space radiation.

Working in JPL’s Environmental Test Laboratory, engineers bent the antenna to simulate one possible orientation after a SkyFall flight at Mars. Then they ran it through dramatic thermal shifts to simulate the Martian day-night cycle, during which temperatures can swing by as much as 170 degrees Fahrenheit (94 degrees Celsius). Next, they repeatedly flexed the antenna as if it had gone through dozens of landings. Along the way, they paused six times to carry the hardware to an electromagnetic test chamber to verify that its ability to beam and receive radar signals hadn’t diminished.

During radiofrequency testing, the team inverted the antenna so that the bottom pointed up — a setup that stresses the structure more than Mars’ one-third gravity ever would — and tested signal performance. By the end of the test campaign, the antenna had withstood 200 Mars landings, more than double what would be required for a successful prime mission, with no loss of performance.

“This test checked every box it was supposed to and answered our biggest technical questions,” said Tang. “While we still have work ahead of us before the antenna is fully flight-qualified, this was a major milestone, and the hardware performed exactly as expected.”

With the antenna’s first big test campaign behind it, the ground-penetrating radar team is building an engineering model that will endure vibration testing, deployment in a simulated Martian environment, signal testing, and outdoor trials at JPL’s Mars Yard.

Equipped with four instruments each, the three SkyFall aircraft follow in the footsteps of NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, which flew 72 times over nearly three years, proving that powered, controlled flight is possible in the rarefied Martian atmosphere. It also demonstrated how an aerial perspective can generate valuable data by helping NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover team plan time-saving routes and choose locations for science-gathering.
SkyFall is expected to launch aboard NASA’s Space Reactor-1 Freedom in late 2028.

Rockets vibrate, shake, and flex intensely as they climb into space, and spacecraft packed with delicate scientific instruments must survive those forces. Before any rocket leaves the ground, NASA engineers work to predict how those stresses will affect every part of a spacecraft.

To do that, engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group with NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida have streamlined how they ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces, strengthening mission safety in the process.

Using a commercial digital software tool in a new way, the engineers developed a standardized modeling workflow for finite element modeling to strengthen shock and vibration analysis and ensure hardware is prepared for the extreme environments of launch and ascent.

“This computer-based method helps predict how rockets and spacecraft behave under extreme conditions before hardware is built and helps identify weak spots and potential failure risks early so the team can address the findings,” said Brian Beaver, chief of the Flight Analysis Division with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy.

The team recently used the software for the first time while certifying a commercial launch provider’s rocket selected for a NASA mission. The commercial partner provided vibration testing but not shock testing. The Dynamic Environments Group determined shock testing was needed and used a template the group created to run what-if comparisons, visualize structural behavior, and answer complex questions that would have required extensive manual modeling in the past. The team verified the company’s testing results for flight environments, and the analysis provided new insights addressing shock during transport.

“We are using a tool that’s existed for decades, but it’s not normally used by the dynamic environments disciplines,” said Alex Hardt, aerospace engineer with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy. “But we’re changing that. We’re using it in a relatively new area of dynamics.”
Although rockets and spacecraft are designed to absorb shocks and vibrations, those forces can cause wear and tear or potentially flight failures, especially during launch and ascent.

“We define how severe the random vibration levels and shock levels are, and then we verify that all the parts going on future rockets have been tested to those levels, maximizing their longevity,” Hardt said.

For decades, engineers have estimated shock and vibration environments using rules of thumb or by scaling previous data to estimate how each rocket component or spacecraft equipment would be impacted once assembled and flown. The approach worked, but relied heavily on engineering judgment and simple approximations drawn from past missions.

Because most dynamic environments engineers use finite element modeling tools infrequently, they often need to re-learn complex workflows. The software replaces older tools and provides a standard template that guides engineers more quickly and thoroughly through vibration profiles and shock conditions.

Finite element analysis is a powerful simulation technique that breaks a complex structure into smaller components so computers can accurately predict how a spacecraft or rocket could respond to specific forces or launch environments. This is important because issues can be addressed on the ground; once the rocket leaves the launch pad, most problems cannot be repaired or corrected, making early identification essential.

“We’ve used it to get really valuable insight very quickly into verifying a provider’s system,” Hardt said. “It’s already provided some really deep insight into something that normally takes a lot of effort.”

Hardt says having the ability to visualize non-intuitive dynamics problems using finite element models also highlights the software’s valuable impact on learning, efficiency, and alignment with NASA’s people focused culture. The workflow can help the engineers share knowledge, refine assessments with additional flight data, and increase proficiency with modeling tools. This capability already has saved months by allowing the team to run analysis independently without having to request and wait for analysis reports or data, and by helping them identify risks that weren’t previously considered.

NASA’s Launch Services Program Office is responsible for launching rockets delivering spacecraft that observe the Earth, visit other planets and explore the universe, from weather satellites to space telescopes to Mars rovers. The team is constantly adopting new tools like this to give the agency the highest practical chance of success for each mission.

If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed in his 1492 postmortem inventory. Guns and gunpowder were controversial. In art and literature, they were labelled the Devil’s work, and were perceived as fundamentally unchivalrous. Yet within half a century, by the early months of 1539, Lorenzo’s descendant Duke Cosimo de’ Medici had 91 firearms in his Florentine storerooms. Somehow, in the courts of late-Renaissance Italy, the gun had become an acceptable, even valued, weapon.

Beyond the palazzi of the peninsula’s towns and cities, guns were also making inroads into more ordinary lives. There were no standing armies in the 16th-century Italian states. Their wars were fought through temporary mobilisations, and with considerable help from companies of mercenaries. Yet as the 1506 provision that established the Florentine militia made clear, ‘little hope’ could be placed ‘in foreign and hired arms’. Far better to establish a new magistracy with ‘full authority and power’ to enlist men from Florentine territory, at least 10,000 of them. One in 10 of these men were to be equipped with firearms, and 500 handguns (schioppetti) should be kept in the Palazzo della Signoria (the city hall, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio) along with ‘such money as should be necessary for the schioppetti’, presumably to purchase gunpowder and shot. Three or four companies (bandiere) entirely of schioppettieri might also be established.

This militia, most often noted for the role of Niccolò Machiavelli in its foundation, was to be organised after the fashion of the Germans, in whose cities there was a centuries-old tradition of civic defence and a duty on every male citizen to maintain suitable arms for the purpose. In fact, one of the Florentine militia’s early constables was German (a Giovanni Tedesco); another (Giliberto Spagnolo) came from Spain, a country making the running in the use of small arms on the battlefield. Giovanni Tedesco arranged target practice for his company, which from 1508 was extended more generally among the militia, with exercises taking place on a monthly basis.

Militias were not new but, by the 1490s, large-scale foreign military intervention on the Italian peninsula was giving a new impetus to their development, as was the growing importance of infantry in the military context. In Friuli, where Venetian lands bordered Ottoman territory, the militia were using handguns from the 1490s, and city guards across the Italian peninsula were soon provided with guns too. The growth of militias was the single most important factor in the proliferation of firearms in 16th-century Italy. This is too early a period for the kind of autobiographical writing that would tell us what these men made of the process, but there was certainly ample encouragement to become familiar with firearms and acquire shooting skills.

The backdrop to these developments was the decades of war in which France and Spain contended for hegemony on the Italian Peninsula. In the 1480s, while pitching his services to the duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci, highlighting his potential as a military engineer, wrote:

I have also plans of mortars most convenient and easy to carry with which to hurl small stones in the manner almost of a storm; and with the smoke of this cause great terror to the enemy and great loss and confusion.

By the turn of the century, Spanish arquebusiers – named for the long, wooden-stocked gun with which they were armed – were doing precisely that on the battlefields of Italy. As the conflicts of 1494-1559 rolled on, the rulers of the peninsula’s multiple states promoted shooting in the interests of civic defence and military preparedness and, as they did, their own use of firearms shifted too.

The Medici were not the only leading family of Renaissance Italy to take an interest in this new military technology. In 1538, the duke of another Italian city-state, Urbino, described a novel firearm as ‘very dear to me’. Such appreciation, however, ran counter to the dominant image of guns in the period’s literature. Leonhard Fronsperger, once a captain of the ducal armoury in Munich, wrote of gunpowder as ‘indispensable’, but also as ‘horrible’ and ‘unmanly’. Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem Orlando Furioso (1532) described guns as a ‘foul and pestilent discovery’, weapons through which ‘no more shall gallantry, no more shall valour prove their prowess’. Only in edgier texts, like the swashbuckling memoirs of the goldsmith and sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, did anyone hint that guns were fun. ‘Frightened’ by a plague that hit Rome in the early 1520s causing thousands of deaths, Cellini ‘began to seek relief in a sport that I found very enjoyable’. In between sketching the city’s ancient ruins, he shot pigeons. He developed his own gunpowder recipe, and boasted of his ‘really good marksmanship’, claiming to be able to shoot ‘200 yards point-blank’. This is probably exaggerated, but just as relevant is Cellini’s explanation that, by getting him out into the fresh air to go hunting, and combating his ‘naturally melancholy disposition’, his gun ‘brought me more gain than loss’.

The textual enthusiasm of both Cellini and the duke of Urbino finds a material counterpart in a growing culture of luxury weapons. The aesthetics of these high-end guns helped firearms fit into a court culture that valued beauty and craftsmanship. They were decorated with classical gods, Christian figures and mottoes, and images of the hunt, while the novelty value of combination weapons such as spears with miniature guns attached appealed to the Renaissance sense of fun.

Records of gun ownership in elite households, too, tell a different story from the literary sources. It is at court that wheellock guns – a groundbreaking technology that allowed concealed carry – first leave traces. Leonardo’s sketches of their mechanisms (probably developed in Germany) can be seen in the Codex Atlanticus. Expensive, convenient and modern, wheellocks seem to have become a status symbol. The standard military firearm of this period, the matchlock, was fired by means of a lighted cord (the match) that ignited the powder when the gun was triggered. But the wheellock was a self-lighting mechanism that avoided the need for a lighted match. It was a more complex and therefore more expensive technology, and could be unreliable (probably especially if produced on the cheap). On the other hand, wheellocks had advantages in hunting, avoiding as they did the glow and smell of the burning match cord which might alert prey to a hunter’s presence.
Designs echoed court imagery: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, biblical figures

By the start of 1539, Duke Cosimo de’ Medici owned four wheellock handguns made in the German style that he (or more likely his bodyguards) took with him when he travelled. Not a decade on, a wheellock appeared in the first portrait of a European ruler with a handgun: Titian’s equestrian portrait of the victorious Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, in which Charles is shown ‘in the manner in which he went against the rebels’, that is, in the garb of the wheellock-toting Spanish cavalry.

The aesthetic qualities of high-end firearms helped guns blend into the wider courtly environment. Designs echoed imagery common to the court: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, or biblical figures like Judith. A wheellock pistol made in Germany and dated 1548 features a figure of the Roman heroine Lucretia along with a Christian motto and image of the Crucifixion. By this time, guns were finding new uses in Europe’s religious wars: far from the Devil’s weapon, they were a means of asserting true Christianity against the heretics.

Back at court, novelty weapons such as the match-fired combination pollaxe and gun in the Royal Armouries, or the boar-spear with two small guns attached given to Cosimo de’ Medici, engaged with a fashion for wider theatrical and festival machines aimed at provoking wonder in their audience. These firearms functioned as marketing devices, promoting their makers – and perhaps also the cities or states of their makers – as potential providers too of the thousands of weapons that might be commissioned for use in war. A striking indication of their acceptability in elite culture comes in 1553, when Mantuan officials began to make ceremonial presents of firearms to the city’s duke in place of the crossbows they had previously given. That the gun could now appear in these ritual contexts shows it had truly arrived.

In wider society, luxury decoration was out of reach, but other factors favoured an expansion of gun ownership. Florence was not the only state to establish or revive a civic militia. In the context of long-running on-off war, it made sense for rulers across Italy to mobilise citizens and equip them with up-to-date weapons. Alongside requirements for militia drill went contests to incentivise the acquisition of shooting skills. Farmers found guns useful for pest control; hunters used them too. Thus, in the 1520s and beyond, more and more Italian states formalised or expanded their militia. Giovanni Moro, a Venetian official who had previously handled military supplies, proposed in 1525 the formation of a citizen militia of 12,000 men, of whom two-thirds would use firearms; these men would receive powder and lead for practice, and a contest would be held three times a year to encourage them. This would be, said Moro, to the ‘honour and utility’ of Venice, and of ‘great benefit’ when it came to conserving Venetian territory.

Such ambitious plans didn’t always succeed, as two cases from Tuscany show. Jacopo Pessina’s detailed study of military organisation in the Republic of Siena estimates that in the last 30 years of the republic (1525-55), between 20 and 33 per cent of adult men served in the militia, with each 500-strong battalion including 150-200 arquebusiers. A report from 1543, however, suggested that the militia was not fit for purpose, lacking not only sufficient men but also the necessary firearms and helmets. The case of Florence, moreover, where the last republican government of 1527-30 fell to the Spanish-backed Medici party after a long siege, shows the limits of a city militia in the face of a foreign army. Anticipating attack, the republican government issued new ordinances for the militia, instituting training in the use of arquebuses, and shooting contests. During the siege of 1530, artisans from shoemakers to cutlers were equipped with arquebuses. They did not, however, prevail against the much better-resourced Spanish army. Still, governments across Italy continued to expand their militia, which made firearms increasingly available to men of all social ranks.
‘Every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’

If militia service provided one route to familiarity with firearms, so did the related rise of shooting contests. In 1506, Venice introduced a competition to encourage the development of handgun skills among the archers serving on its naval galleys. In 1518, the first prize was 16 arms-lengths of damask fabric, worth 32 ducats, along with 6 ducats in cash. In 1520, the Republic of Lucca instituted a thrice-yearly shooting contest in order to ensure that its citizens were prepared for defence, the founding decree urging them to prefer ‘death over the loss of dear liberty and the reduction of their fatherland to servitude’. Prizes included a silver cup worth almost 20 ducats, and six arms-lengths of damask worth 5 ducats. Soldiers’ pay could be less than 30 ducats a year, so these were generous rewards. Contests, however, were not only about financial incentives. They were also about establishing an acceptable social image for the firearm, just as the iconography of luxury weapons had done at court. The language of the Lucca decree, for example, offered a new and more positive discourse of the gun, as a weapon for the defence of liberty.

Hunting was another context in which guns became familiar not just for elites but more widely. In 1552, for example, a cowherd named Vincenzo obtained a licence from the Bologna authorities that allowed him to carry arms, including a gun for the purpose of hunting. It came with the standard caveat that the weapon must not be carried in churches, at festivals or in markets. These were busy environments where an accidental misfire had higher risks than out in the countryside, and where a generalised ban on arms-bearing (staff weapons such as pikes were also included) made policing more straightforward. Such wide access to guns, however, was a matter of concern. The anonymous author of a proposition for international gun control observed, probably in the late 1570s, that if the Italian princes did not take action soon, then ‘there will be no place nor state where people are safe, given that every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’.

As guns became more common, so did their appearance in the criminal records. By 1600, firearms had become the predominant weapon used to commit homicide in Bologna. That said, they still accounted for only a third of offences, and in interpreting the figures we should bear in mind the relative lethality of guns when compared with other weapons. In fact, across the broad range of gun crime, it was still relatively rare to come across cases where guns were directly used in planned homicide. More commonly, they were used to threaten: the ideal outcome for the highwayman who shouts: ‘Your money or your life!’ is to ride away with the money without firing a shot.

Many of the historic investigations feature possession of illegal guns and/or their use to intimidate. In a 1554 case near the northern Italian city of Brescia, Valerio Soncino and a gang of 20 men ‘armed with various weapons, including arquebuses’, scaled the walls of a property belonging to Valerio’s brother Annibale, and ‘with various threats’ forced two of his stewards to bring them carts, which they loaded up with goods, stealing in addition cattle and a horse. The robbers got only five miles, however, before they were halted by some villagers who had got wind of what was happening and sounded the alarm. In the ensuing violence, two men and a woman among the villagers were injured. Here, the primary use of the guns was to frighten people into doing as they were told, not to kill them. That is not to say, however, that the proliferation of firearms was not risky. Criminal records from Bologna describe a case in 1575 in which an elderly woman named Giovanna was killed by a man named Pierantonio Fangarezzo; Fangarezzo had been looking over an arquebus (perhaps an early variety of flintlock) to see how it worked when it accidentally went off.
In some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership

People engaged in, or considering, political violence also used firearms. The distinction between criminal and political activity was not always straightforward. The system of exile in the Italian states – in which offenders were banned from their home territory and had their property confiscated – often made banditry an attractive option (hence the overlap between the concepts in Italian, where the word bandito is also used for an exile). Civic authorities were particularly keen to police weapon ownership when it posed a risk to the regime. The early years of Medici ducal rule in Florence (formally established in 1532) saw numerous confiscations of illegal weapons: Girolamo di Filippo Bonciani and Francesco di Piero Serragli, for example, fell foul of the law after an arquebus was found under the straw of their former stable. Some of these weapons were probably planted by city officials, but opponents of the regime might reasonably have decided to arm themselves in case of an uprising (for which there were several precedents).

Dissidents in Brescia (a subject city of Venice) also obtained weapons: testimony from 1539 shows how one alleged firearm offender, Antonio Maria, was accused of saying several times that ‘he desired nothing more than that the Emperor and the King of France should make an accord against our Venetian lords, and that he hoped to come with them to sack Brescia.’ Antonio Maria was further accused of ‘continually keeping in his house exiled men of a bad sort, who go out killing on the streets’; he had in his house around 25 guns of different types. While we typically learn about these cases from regime records, by reading between the lines it becomes clear that at least in some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership.

People in northern and central Italy owned guns for several reasons: to participate in militia service, for hunting and livestock control, and for criminal activity. Some of this ownership was purely practical: a gun would more reliably than the alternatives kill the fox eating your chickens. Some of it had political motivations, whether to defend the liberty of one’s own fatherland or to oppose a tyrannical overlord. By the middle of the 16th century, a lot of people had guns. It is challenging to establish quite how many. Based on population estimates and numbers enrolled in the militia, the historians Michael Mallett and John Hale estimated that one in 15 rural households in Venetian territory would have had a firearm following the establishment of the militia in the later 1520s: ‘the government’, they observed in Military Organisation of a Renaissance State (2009), ‘was calculatedly accepting a risk to public order’. By 1540, the ruler of Modena required that one in three countryside households should have a gun. These calculations concern militia service, however, and other people may have bought guns second-hand from soldiers, or won them via gambling.

Later in the century, larger cities had shops where guns might be mended and probably also purchased. A 1559 proclamation issued in Bologna in anticipation of riots declared that ‘shopkeepers, who sell those polearms and arquebuses, must store them in their shops in such a way that they are not ready to use’. There is no reason to think that the anonymous author who complained of wheellock-toting shepherds was greatly exaggerating the extent of proliferation.
Guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership

Certain moments in wartime no doubt accelerated access to firearms. Besides the 1529-30 Siege of Florence, records of the defensive provisions in Ferrara of 1552 (when the city was likewise preparing for a possible siege) show that, out of 520 households equipped with armour, pikes, arquebuses and morions, more than half (270) had a gun. Included in this list are 18 female heads of household, of whom six had guns. This raises the question of how many women were gun-owners more generally. The answer seems to be rather few. Sieges were emergency situations in which gender norms might temporarily be suspended, such as when the women of Siena took responsibility for repairs to the city walls. Outside the wartime context, Joe Tryner’s study of court records in Bologna turned up only a single example of a woman with a firearm, and nothing in my wider survey of source material has suggested that was untypical.

In contrast, guns did come to be associated with masculinity. In The Fruit of Liberty (2013), Nicholas Scott Baker argued that the siege of 1529-30 was a particular turning point for elite identity, redefining notions of masculinity from those associated with practices of civic governance to something more ‘rugged, militaristic’. This was particularly apparent in changing clothing styles, to which the bearing of new types of arms might be added. Focusing on Florence after 1537, in Masculinity, Arms and Armour (2020), Victoria Bartels identifies guns as one factor in shifting performances of masculinity, noting that they increased the danger attached to ‘routine bouts of aggression’ that had traditionally been employed to settle disputes between men. In the context of the Italian Wars (and specific local conflicts within them), guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership. This is confirmed in the account of Benvenuto Cellini, whose self-aggrandising narrative of his participation in the Italian Wars includes a comment he made to a companion, Alessandro del Bene, to persuade him to stick around and shoot back at an invading army during the 1527 Sack of Rome: ‘Now you’ve brought me here, we must show that we’re men.’

Over the course of the 16th century, familiarity with firearms grew. It was increasingly expected that men would be able to use a gun: the expansion of militias was a key factor here alongside direct soldiering experience. The acquisition of skills in shooting was positively encouraged through civic contests with generous prizes. Rhetoric about the importance of guns for civic defence and for the maintenance of honour and liberty offered a counterweight to more negative images of gunpowder weapons as diabolical, unchivalrous or impious. Guns were useful for protection of livestock from predators as well as for hunting more generally. In turn, their ready availability also made them accessible for use by bandits, during vendettas and indeed for political violence. However, their lethality shifted the dynamics of violent encounters: so effective were guns as a threat that in some cases they may have prompted victims to give up without a fight. On the other hand, with increasing proliferation came an increased risk of both accidents and casual use in interpersonal violence. Yet not all gun ownership was enthusiastic. Some applicants for arms licences evidently felt constrained to carry guns in self-defence, and cultural ambivalence about these weapons remained long after they became common objects.
As firearms became more familiar, it was as much a decision not to be a gun owner as to acquire the new technology.

That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film.

Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it was a matter of time before co-CEO Ted Sarandos would show Lin the door.

It took a day. On the heels of the Bajaria news on Thursday, Sarandos rang Lin on Friday to tell him he’d been dismissed, three sources told Variety. The exec kept his head up and pressed on through the weekend, appearing at Saturday’s Academy Gala (in the same room as Sarandos) and at a Sunday tastemaker screening to support the filmmakers of “La Bola Negra.” As has been summarized in many articles about the Netflix purge, creative leadership at the company is being overhauled amid poor stock performance and declining user engagement on the platform. Peter Rice, the veteran film and TV executive, will now preside over and shake up the platform’s content.

Competing narratives are flying about why Lin was let go, but they arrive at the same conclusion: In the end, it wasn’t working. Some say Sarandos is desperate to sell a story about growth to Wall Street (Netflix’s quarterly earnings report drops Tuesday). Others say Lin could not dance fast enough to find the balance between sticky streaming titles and theatrical release experiments (in fairness, he made it halfway through a five-year deal, barely enough time to get a casting announcement together by today’s standards). There are also some interesting leaks around tension he’s said to have with A-list filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck, which we’ll get to.

The Lin era at Netflix was framed around austerity, both by the town and in some ways by “The Lego Movie” producer himself. A June profile in the New York Times declared Lin was done “coddling” Hollywood, bragging he did not “fawn over stars or write blank checks.” The implication was that his predecessor Scott Stuber had overpaid for talent and too-ambitiously committed to a new Netflix movie release every week in 2022. Those efforts scaled back gradually until Stuber exited in mid-2024.

Lin entered with a red pen and a machete, the lore goes, in hopes of emphasizing quality over quantity. Some find it convenient that Stuber’s legacy is still being kicked up, perhaps to provide cloud cover for decisions made by Lin and his former boss Bajaria. Amid the noise of the current Netflix layoffs, it’s important to remember that the prevailing logic at Netflix for a long, long time was “we don’t give a shit about theatrical,” said one colorful studio source. Releasing movies in theaters was never part of the Netflix business model. Stuber paid premiums to get filmmakers like Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón and Rian Johnson on the service.
